title: Milburn Creek and Bedell's Landing Vicinity
summary: Milburn Creek and the Bedell's Landing area are part of a wider Freeport-Baldwin shoreline landscape where local histories remember Merrick maritime life, shellfishing, wampum-making materials, and stone implements found near the creek.
address_label: Milburn Pond Park / Milburn Creek Park, West Merrick Road and South Brookside Avenue, Freeport, NY
map_geometry_source: Nassau County facility record 25, Milburn Pond Park / Milburn Creek Park: West Merrick Road and South Brookside Avenue; official facility map 40.6513902671482, -73.6017556478041, consulted September 12, 2026.
ancestral_territory_note: Within and near Merrick ancestral land; connected to the broader creek-and-bay landscape.
why_this_matters: Milburn Creek carries the history of Meroke fishing and shoreline life alongside later changes to the waterway. Looking from today’s public park connects that longer history with the ponds, roads and neighborhoods people know now.
introduction_title: A Creek, Bay, and Shellfishing Landscape
introduction_content:
Milburn Creek linked the uplands, marshes, and bay waters along the Freeport-Baldwin border. Local Baldwin histories describe large clam-shell deposits along the creek banks, shell materials used for wampum, and stone implements found over time.1

The creek-and-bay landscape carries Merrick maritime history through shellfishing, shoreline travel, wampum economies, and long relationships with the south shore marshes.2
history_title: Shellfishing, settlement and a changing creek
history_content:
Nineteenth-century local accounts say that visible shell deposits in the Bedell's Landing area were later removed for fertilizer. The memory of those deposits still points to generations of coastal harvest, travel, and work along the water.1

Cow Meadow, Freeport Creek, Baldwin Bay, and Hick's Neck marshes are best understood as connected parts of this south shore cultural landscape.2

1686: a mill reshapes the waterway

Baldwin Historical Society places Meroke life along Milburn Creek and records John Pine’s first gristmill in 1686. Read together, these histories show the creek as both an Indigenous fishing landscape and a waterway altered by colonial settlement.2

From a lived waterway to a mill landscape

Milburn Creek connected Meroke fishing and shell-working with the bays of the South Shore. Baldwin Historical Society places Meroke people along the creek and describes the making of wampum for exchange. The waterway belonged to a network of food, work, and relationships before it became a source of power for settlers’ mills.2

The mill established by John Pine in 1686 helped attract farms and businesses. Later accounts describe salt-marsh hay cutting, clamming, and shipping in the surrounding bay landscape. Reading these changes together makes the creek more than a former industrial site: it shows how newcomers reorganized access to a waterway already important to Native life. Merrick Road connects this creek history with the older routes across the coast.2
whereintheworld_title: See the waterway from a public park
whereintheworld_content:
Begin at Milburn Pond Park / Milburn Creek Park, at West Merrick Road and South Brookside Avenue. This public park provides a place to look at the waterway within the broader Freeport–Baldwin creek landscape.3

County park information and location · Continue to Merrick history.3
